newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss report on Holocaust funds pushed back a week.
newsitem.headline: Swiss report on Holocaust funds pushed back a week.

text.p: Switzerland's official report on whether its citizens pocketed unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims as compensation for nationalised property in eastern Europe has been delayed around a week, Berne said on Tuesday.

Thomas Borer, head of the task force aimed at mending damage to Switzerland's reputation from allegations that the neutral Swiss cynically profited from World War Two, said the report from two independent historians would not appear on Wednesday as planned.
He told Reuters the historians' work had taken longer than first scheduled but had made good progress. "The report is very comprehensive and may well appear next week," he said.
Switzerland, pressed by foreign critics, pledged in October to answer by December 4 accusations it used Holocaust victims' riches to compensate Swiss citizens for their seized property.

The foreign ministry named two Swiss historians to examine compensation deals reached after World War Two with the then-communist regimes of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Romania and Hungary.
Peter Hug, one of the historians, told Reuters the report was practically finished but declined to discuss its contents. He said it only needed to be translated and printed.
"There are some technical problems but it is basically done," he said.
Borer, troubleshooter for Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, has said it was possible that the historians' findings could lead to political consequences but has declined to elaborate.
Switzerland has struggled to cope with a flood of criticism from world Jewish groups about the way it handled accounts left ownerless by murdered Jews and other victims of Nazi oppression.

The controvery was fuelled by the rediscovery of a 1949 deal with Poland that allowed Warsaw to pay off Swiss claims for nationalised property through a clearing account funded in part by Poles' unclaimed Swiss bank accounts and insurance policies.
Switzerland gave Poland around 480,000 Swiss francs ($362,000) under the accord. Berne also earmarked 325,000 francs in dormant assets for Hungary under a similar pact.
Berne has not yet said whether dormant accounts were also used in compensation treaties with other communist states.
Jewish groups say much of the dormant money in the pact with Poland was deposited by Jews killed in the Holocaust.

Berne is also setting up a broad historical enquiry into Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre. Swiss banks and Jewish groups are also probing the fate of dormant accounts. ($1=1.3260 Swiss Franc)
